name: – Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy – § 146 – Am 57
title: REPORT on discharge in respect of the implementation of the general budget of the European Union for the financial year 2024, Section I – European Parliament
part_text: 146. Welcomes the publication of Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2025/2445 of the European Parliament and of the Council5 , which introduces new requirements for European political parties and European political foundations with the aim of strengthening democratic integrity and resilience; underlines in particular that European political parties now also have to ensure compliance of their member parties, and European political foundations of their member organisations, with the values on which the Union is founded as enshrined in Article 2 of the TEU; further notes that safeguards against foreign interference have been reinforced, and that the revised sanctions system requires sanctions for quantifiable infringements – such as breaches of donation rules or the prohibition on providing funding to national parties – to be imposed without offering an opportunity for corrective measures; positively notes in this context the comprehensive preventive guidance offered by the Authority with its Regulatory Compliance Action Plan ('R-CAP') so as to facilitate smooth and effective implementation; encourages the decision to introduce eligibility checks also within member organisations, in order to ensure full coherence of also the member organisations with the values of Article 2 TEU and to uphold democratic integrity in Parliament’s funding of European Political parties; in this regard, is concerned that certain European political parties6a (primarily donations received by ALDE from Microsoft, Vodafone, etc.) and European political foundations6b (donations received by the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies from Janssen Pharmaceutica, Apple, Google, etc., by George Soros’s Open Society for the Foundation for European Progressive Studies and for the Green European Foundation, by Google, Janssen, Apple, Microsoft, Vodafone, for the European Liberal Forum, etc.) are partly funded by major IT, pharmaceutical, and other groups—whose parent companies are notably American—which could be equated with lobbying and thus suggest some influence on the legislative process or contribution to election campaigns; thus warns against potential conflicts of interest that could arise from this legal situation, albeit ethically questionable, particularly when members of these political groups serve as rapporteurs on dossiers relating to these sectors;
